utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, on the screen you have this document marked P3, which you were shown by the Prosecutor. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. The document which is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that you were shown by the Prosecutor. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Transcript 30th of August, 5th of September, on several occasions you said or you objected to the format of the document because you said that there was no seal, that there was no proper number, registration number, or a log number. Before you, you have a different document, P869, and this is more or less of identical content as the other document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document, P869 has a proper log number and calls upon the statute of Kljuc Municipality, has a seal, and it has Jovo Banjac's signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that this document too has something that you would object to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to object to because in January 1992 we were not in the municipal assembly, so they were able to implement this. But while we were in the assembly, they were not able to implement this, to have this passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, Mr. Filipovic, about the format. Is there something in this document P869, is there something that you object to in terms of format?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing to object to except that this was passed without the participation of citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the participation in power, and you looked at a document from January 1992 and you said that it was from January 1992 that you no longer took part in the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We declared the Bosnian Kljuc or proclaimed the Bosnian Kljuc in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This proclamation, P870, that you read a while ago, which is in relation to the press conference given by your late brother, is dated from the 30th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't want to understand what I'm saying. We officially proclaimed it, and then with the Serbian side we cooperated as the assembly of the town, and we had meetings and all that but our intention was that the assembly from the elections of 1990, that this was the town's assembly and these were the kind of contacts that we had with the authorities. We believed that the town of Kljuc was one thing. There are two municipalities. They have their own; we have our own. And that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I kindly ask you and would like to warn you to answer my question so that we don't waste time any more. The document P870, which you looked at a moment ago, the very first sentence says: "At yesterday's session of the deputy's club of the SDA and MBO a new municipality was declared of Bosnian Kljuc." And the date is the 30th of January, 1992. Did you declare or proclaim the Municipality of Bosnian Kljuc on that session of the 29th of January, 1992 or before that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep asking me. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was winter. I can't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if on the 16th of January, 1992 you took part in the authorities in the division of power in the Municipality of Kljuc; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Zecevic, until the break-up -- I cannot remember the date. Until the break-up I was a deputy at the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc. And the day of the break-up we then had our sessions, the Serbs had their own sessions. And I think that on a couple of occasions we met to discuss some things but I cannot remember the dates. Don't ask me about dates. I know only a couple of dates. And in everything I say, I said "around such and such a date."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I completely accept this. Of course ten years have passed. So I'm not asking about specific dates. But you said a moment ago when you were looking at document P869, this decision, you said -- the document is dated 6th of January, 1992, and you said it was the Serbs who passed -- adopted this decision, and already then you were not participating in the authorities in power.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying, the decision was passed, adopted without us. But again, don't hang onto the dates, because I know only a couple of dates that are only important to me for personal reasons and some other dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I completely understand. Mr. Filipovic, regardless of the fact that, as you say, you did not take part in the authorities, you didn't participate in power, you kept the functions or the positions that you had in the municipal assembly. Your late brother, Omer, as vice-president; Asim Egrlic as the president of the executive committee; Botenic as the president of the court and others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An that went on until May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From May 1992 onwards, you said in your testimony and in your statements that as a protest you did not want to take part in power so that you would leave or walk out of sessions and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of sessions? In May? That May you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sessions of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were no sessions in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, if there weren't any -- I know that there weren't any in May because it was practically war. 7th of May, there was the takeover of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me in terms of positions, say, of your late brother. Until what time did he carry out the function of vice-president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just -- until just before the war. Until the session just before the war. But this was just a pro forma function, position. He was not actually able to carry out his position, duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say until the beginning of the war, what date do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 25th of May. So in spite of the fact that as the police was taken over on the 7th, your brother, as the vice-president of the assembly, and all others were still continuing to carry out their duties in assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when we would go to our work in front of the municipality building there were two policemen standing there, and one was a soldier, an army member, and they would only search Muslims and Croats, while Serbs passed through normally. While here, when you go into the Tribunal, everyone is being searched. While in the municipality, only Muslims and Croats were searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I would like to ask you again, please could you answer my question. I didn't ask you about searches. I asked you whether your late brother and others went --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered your question. I said yes, but we had certain problems, so allow me to say this. I said yes, but there were a few details that I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say that your brother was the vice-president, but he didn't have any direct duties since Jovo Banjac was the president; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But Asim Egrlic was the president of the executive board, which really was the main executive authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the president of the executive board, but Mr. Asim Egrlic didn't ask about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the executive board adopted any decisions in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. All I know is that they had coffee together in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document P905, please. Your Honours, there is a problem with this document. Actually, it is -- it has been marked as a P905, and it does contain actually three different documents. I don't know whether -- whether should we give -- if the -- if the Prosecutor does not object, maybe we should give it a /1, /2, /3 or something. Because it actually is three different decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I've no objection if -- to be marked with a .1, which would be the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Level of payments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- level of payment. .2 would be the decision on payment of tax, and 3 -- .3, to extend the validity of federal and republican regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll take note of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness be shown 905/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm only interested in the bottom of the document. The date is the 12th of May, 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the signature is the signature of Asim Egrlic, the chairman. Sir, the same question for this document. The 12th of May -- that's the date, the 12th of May. And it's signed by the chairman of the executive committee, Asim Egrlic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 905/3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document also bears the date the 12th of May, 1992, and it's also been signed by the chairman of the executive committee, Asim Egrlic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this is a decision to extend the validity of federal and republican regulations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the ARK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, item 1 states the following: "Until the introduction of specific regulations for the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, regulations issued in the SFRJ, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the SRBH, before the 7th of April, 1992 that do not contravene the constitution and laws of the Serbian Republic of BH will be applied. Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That document was signed by the chairman of the executive committee Asim Egrlic on the 12th of May, who was also the president of the SDA in Kljuc; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, does this mean that Asim Egrlic accepted the existence of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask him. On the basis of the document that he has signed, I would say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in a certain manner, members of the Muslim people continued to participate in the power structure in the course of 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You should ask Mr. Egrlic. Ask Mr. Egrlic about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Thank you. In the course of the testimony that you gave here, you mentioned that Muslims in Kljuc had been in danger in 1992, that they were in danger in 1992, and you said that you and your late brother at a press conference also wore yellow ribbons, if I remember correctly. And in that part of your testimony, you said that in your opinion they were implementing the plan of a certain doctor called Stevan Moljevic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since I don't know about this gentleman, I heard about him for the first time from you. Could you tell me, were you really familiar with Dr. Moljevic's alleged plan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Moljevic's plan, the greater Serbia was supposed to go from Karlovac to Karlobag. This was supposed to be the border, down towards Zagreb. That's as far as this greater Serbia was to reach. And the front lines, the front lines were more or less within those limits. The borders that Moljevic had imagined as being those of the greater Serbia. That's why Slovenia left Yugoslavia, because in his -- according to his ideas, Slovenia was not to be part of the greater Serbia. Part of Croatia was not to be part of the greater Serbia. So wherever there was fighting, that's where this was irrelevant. I can't talk about this without documents and maps, but the war was waged in the areas where he imagined Greater Serbia to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what his attitude was towards that plan and with regard to members of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What his attitude was, what his position was, I don't know. But I do know what the position was towards the Muslims, what it was like about 100 years ago, several hundred years ago. And I also know how the Serbian authorities treated Muslims. You consider us to be Turks. The Serbian authorities consider us to be Turks. We have nothing to do with the Turks. The Turks are Turks and we're Bosnians of Islam faith. But when the war started in Bosnia, they'd say, "Kill a Turk. Kill a Turk." I've got nothing to do with any Turk, so go back into the past, read up on history, you'll see about the Serbs who inhabited Uzice, Belgrade, et cetera. You'll see how many mosques there were in Belgrade itself several hundred years ago and you'll see how many mosques there are there now and you'll see what the situation is in Uzice, et cetera, et cetera. I don't want to discuss history at any -- at any greater left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... leave history behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we'll proceed with the cross-examination. Mr. Zecevic, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I just asked because the witness has mentioned Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And my question was concerning Dr. Moljevic and not the overall history --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Or whatever is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But now please proceed with the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- is the position of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that -- are you familiar with the fact that in -- according to his plan, Dr. Moljevic said that the Muslim people had to be a constituent part of the federal units of Yugoslavia because of the common life that both peoples were used to; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because as far as I know, when Moljevic was alive there was no Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago a colleague showed you the Exhibit P877, which is the opinion of -- on the candidates for judge. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the second page, at the very beginning of the second page in the Serbian version - and it's in the middle of the English version - it says the following: "The SDS, the municipal committee, suggests that for these reasons we suggest only -- and one other judge of Muslim nationality be elected. The SDS proposes that the candidate be Ibro Sehic, who is currently working as a self-management public attorney and whose duties in previous work and behaviour enjoys the confidence of all municipalities." That's what it states; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Ibro Sehic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ibro Sehic is a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a first and last name of a Muslim, and he is a member of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the municipal committee of the SDS in February 1992, which is the date of this document, proposed that a member of the Muslim people be a judge of the municipal court in Kljuc; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, Mr. Zecevic, but at the time I don't know whether Mr. Sehic had passed his judicial law exam, whether he had become a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the second candidate was Nihad Filipovic, a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My uncle's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that Nihad Filipovic was the secretary of the MBO in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see that the municipal committee of the SDS in the third paragraph says: "As far as the other candidates of Muslim nationality is concerned, Nihad Filipovic, the SDS did not support his candidature because he has rather compromised himself politically in his area." Is this correct, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question with a yes or no. If you will allow me to answer the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. I'm not interested in the details, though. I want to know whether Nihad Filipovic, your relative, was a member of a political organisation in Kljuc and I want to know whether he was involved in political activity.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this isn't an answer to your question, but Nihad Filipovic, we are relatives. At that time he was a member of the Liberal Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Its secretary?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was, but he had a high-level position in the Liberal Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had passed his law exam. He had become a candidate for a judge, to become a judge, but he came forth because -- well, I'll just give you an example if Your Honours will allow me to do so. In December when 25 buses of Croats were forced out from Slunj and when they were maltreated in Kljuc by the police, only three Filipovics went to say, "People, stop doing that. It's not correct." Omer Filipovic, Muhamed Filipovic and Nihad Filipovic came out -- came forward to say this. So if this means being prominent, well, yes. People who had a heart, who had a soul, we were the only ones in the entire town who fed people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't want to interrupt the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When answering a question that my colleague put to you, you said that the SDA and MBO Crisis Staff was established in Kljuc. You said that the Crisis Staff of the SDA and the MBO was established sometime around the second half of 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the SDS founded a Crisis Staff only in December 1991, on the 23rd of December?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but they could have done this in December or January 1992 on the basis of documents. But they had a Crisis Staff at a date which was much earlier than 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document P1010, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, all I'm interested in is the date. It's in the first sentence of this document. It's a report on the work of the Crisis Staff. And the document is dated the 29th of July, 1992, and it's from Kljuc. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says, "Report on the work of the Crisis Staff in the period since 15th May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the first sentence in the document, it says: "The Crisis Staff was formed -- was set up by the executive board of the Kljuc Serbian Democratic Party of the 23rd of December, 1991." Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that they had reason -- that some members of the Crisis Staff had reason in July 1992 to state that the Crisis Staff was formed in December 1991, even though this was not correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- can I -- can I make the -- ask the same questions I asked in relation to a document -- the Milos document. According to my records, this document is objected to by the Defence for General Talic on the basis that it doesn't have a signature or seal or whatever. I'm afraid the Defence can't have it both ways. Are they saying that this is an accurate reflection of the events; in other words, that this document is in fact an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're not -- we're not stating at all that this is an authentic document. The fact that the document does reveal the exact date when the Crisis Staff was formed in Kljuc does not mean that the document is authentic. I mean, the contents of this document. So that is why I used it, because that is the only document which we have which refers to this particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No prejudice to its relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the previous instance, in the previous case, I did actually comment that it's neither here nor there and one could take it that it's without prejudice. In your case, you're specifically referring to something fundamental. In other words, you're saying you have here this document which purports to be a document of the Crisis Staff dated July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you see any logic? Could you perhaps try to make us understand why on earth they would have had a reason to say in that document in July 1992 that the Crisis Staff was formed in December 1991. So basically you're referring to the contents of this document and, on the basis of what is contained in that particular paragraph, you are confuting -- you're asking a direct question to the witness. So it -- it is somewhat different from the case of Mr. Trbojevic, when he was referring the witness to the Milos signed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so it's -- just so it's absolutely clear to Mr. Zecevic. You cannot on the one hand assert that this document is not authentic and then on the other try and use the document, as Your Honours just said, to controvert what a witness has said. You have to make a decision as to what is your theory on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is very clear, Your Honours, and my learned colleague. We -- as we have already said, we don't -- do not accept this document as authentic document, and we have stated this many times, why and the reasons. Why I asked this question was because I was provoked by the comment of the -- of the witness, because the witness said, as he used this -- it during his testimony that he was suggesting that a lot of the documents were in some -- some way tampered with, and that was his suggestion. I don't know whether it -- it appeared in the -- in the transcript, but out of the -- because we speak the same language, I understood what was his intention. That is why I asked that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But it still follows, Mr. Zecevic, that if you are still contesting the authenticity of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- then you shouldn't be referring to parts of it and questioning the witness on -- on the validity or otherwise of the statement contained there, unless you are using your question to prove the non-authenticity of the document. If you are putting the question to sustain -- to prove that the witness -- that -- that the document is not authentic, then it's perfectly legitimate. If you are using the document which you contest as being authentic to present or face the witness with a fact in which you then put as being against what is stated earlier, I mean, that's -- that's notice legitimate at all. So you either stop here on -- as far as this document is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And make an affirmation as to whether you are still contesting its authenticity or not, or else decide what you want to do. You know, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. I stated very clearly. I used this document only because of the date, and that was it. No other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, that's not right. Mr. Zecevic put a date to him, said "Were you aware" -- that's how this whole thing started off -- "Were you aware that the Crisis Staff, the Serb Crisis Staff, the SDS Crisis Staff, was only formed on the 23rd of December." "No," said Mr. Filipovic, "I was not. And in my view, it began much earlier." So he's then put -- this document is put only on the basis, as I see it, to show that he's wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, in the course of your testimony you spoke about the fact that your late brother, Omer, was called for a military exercise, I imagine, and he responded to this call. He went there, and three days later he ran away. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the barracks, Zarko Zgonjanin in Prijedor. I couldn't remember the name before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you even issued a declaration if I remember rightly in which you objected. You said it wasn't correct for a party leader to be called for a military exercise.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That meant that if the president of the Muslim Bosniak organisation should go to the reserve forces, why not the president of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether some sort of criminal proceedings had been instituted against your late brother because he left the unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he told the unit commander that he was leaving -- I don't know what rank the commander had and I don't know what he was -- he said, "We can prosecute you." Omer then said, "You can prosecute me. I have political immunity though. You can file charges. I'm quite ready to answer them, because I didn't join the reserve forces in order to watch pornographic films in the course of the day and to drink cognac and to shoot around Kozara in the evening. I just joined the reserve forces." And he said, "Everything that's being done, it's ridiculous."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Any question was whether you knew anything about criminal proceedings being instituted against him.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were instituted against any more Kljuc. I don't know whether something was done in Prijedor, but nothing happened in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Some sort of criminal proceedings were instituted against you, I think, for disrupting public law and order; isn't that correct? You were fined, weren't you? You had to pay a fine; isn't that right? You were found guilty.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not for disrupting law and order. It was a parking fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you received a fine that you had to pay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you are all judges here. I was accused of having attempted to kill a soldier, but the court for misdemeanours cannot deal with proceedings for -- which involved parking, and the witness was a certain Kljajic. He said it wasn't correct, that the charges against me were not correct, and then the judge changed this decision, and I was ordered to pay a fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think there's something I haven't understood. You said that you were accused of having parked incorrectly; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You haven't understood me correctly. I was accused of having parked my car in a certain location. So if Your Honours will allow me to add other things, I parked my car and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to know, Your Honour, what was the offence, Your Honour, nothing else. If he can tell us what -- what was he charged with, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you can't tell us, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was accused of having parked my car incorrectly. The soldier asked me to move the car. I didn't want to, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a physical -- did you physically deal with the soldier then?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We just had a verbal exchange, and that's how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, you spoke or you told us that you established the Bosnian Kljuc municipality, which was a reaction to the Serbian Kljuc initiative.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. At that time Serbs wanted to have everything Serbian, Serbian Kljuc, Serbian Sarajevo, Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbian everything. I don't know what in the former Yugoslavia was not Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if their intention really was to change the name in the Serbian Kljuc, how come it never actually occurred either in 1992 or 1993, 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told us --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just add something? After the end of the war, for a little while there was what was used for the place called Ribnik. It was used as Serbian Kljuc in 1995, 1996. This name was used, Serbian Kljuc, Srpski Kljuc. And then it was abolished, so now it's called again Ribnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript of the 4th of September, page 9517 and further on, you told us in your testimony how some people, allegedly Muslims, would be dismissed from their jobs just because they were Muslims; is that correct? You worked in the municipal administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the municipal surveyor's office, administration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you also passed the state examination for that, you're probably aware of the regulations and the relevant articles of the law to do with employment. You know that according to the law on employment at the time, there was a measure of cessation of employment that if an employee didn't turn up for work for seven days or three days consequently without any reason, he would be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're probably aware that at that time there was a discipline procedure in accordance with the law on employment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there should be a procedure, but I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This discipline procedure was conducted in such a way that the manager would submit a request to the commission, a discipline commission, and then there would be a decision and there would also be a leave for appeal.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it should be according to law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... P1023, 24, 25, 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are starting with which one, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With P1027, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is about a request to start discipline proceedings regarding Smail Dzaferagic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Smail Dzaferagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this was addressed to the discipline commission of the lower court, and this was signed by the president of the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time this was Vlado Dimitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is a decision to form a disciplinary commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Also dated August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is a ruling dated 18th of August, 1992 about the disciplinary responsibility, where there was a ruling for the termination of employment, and this was for certain Eljezovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's for Fedija Eljezovic, a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this document has also instructions, a legal remedy.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me have a look. "An appeal against the decision may be made to the disciplinary commission of the second instance at the high court in Banja Luka within 15 days of the day of receipt." That's what it says, but I don't know what you want me to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just showing you this ruling. That's all. I will ask you a question at the end.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I'll wait then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1025 and 1026 are also rulings, and they are identical to this one but it's to do with different people, so there's no point in me reading from them. But Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me in your opinion, because you looked at the documents, do you believe that according to what you know of the regulations and rules of employment and working for state administration, do you think that this procedure was in accordance with law.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't. No, it wasn't in accordance with law. The rulings were issued in August 1992. The employees were not at work from the 28th of May to the 3rd of June. And in my testimony I said that a mole, an animal that goes underground, could not get through unless it was Serbian. In that time period, from the 28th of May to the 3rd of June, nobody could get through Kljuc without being killed. It was only valid for Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, I asked you only in relation to the procedure, not to the facts?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you. The procedure wasn't respected. It said that it was instruction on legal remedy to appeal to the high court in Banja Luka. That's what it says. Say that this was to do with me, say that I appealed and the appeal would never get to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I lived through this. I felt it on my own skin. I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I remember it well. You were in prison at the time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in prison, but I -- there was a patient in the hospital in Banja Luka, called for a doctor. Instead of a doctor, a nurse would come or a cleaner would come and beat him rather than be looked at by a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, could you tell me, you spoke I believe on two occasions about a certain anonymous letter that was received by your late brother Omer. And we have a copy of it here in the exhibits. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that because of that incident, because of that anonymous letter there was a joint announcement of the SDA and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this only took place after two Muslims were beaten up, and then at the insistence of Jovo Banjac to preserve peace in Kljuc - he called my late brother professor - so he said, "Professor, let's do something." So there was this joint announcement that in the territory of Kljuc there were no White Eagles or Green Berets. It was some kind of political compromise. So it was some kind of a temporary solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... DT27, please. There is English translation as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask. It's one of our documents, I can see, or rather, we have disclosed it, because it bears our numbers. But it's unstamped, sealed, or whatever. Am I taking it being put forward as an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a -- this is not an official document. This is a proclamation which -- which is signed by the -- by the, I think, SDS and SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I -- could I ask the question again: Is it being put forward by the Defence as an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document -- this is not the document that I spoke of earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, under item 1 of this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we proceed, Mr. Zecevic, a little bit differently. Mr. Filipovic, looking at that document, at the bottom, where you have "Za SDA." That's "for SDA." Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems like the signature of Asim Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not to me. Not in the documents which we have seen earlier on today. Which was that document which had 3 and 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 905, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 905. That's the only document I came across today which had the signature of Asim Egrlic. And this is -- doesn't look like it. But I stand to be -- I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, Mr. Egrlic is coming as a witness over here. I assume that he should be asked that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Filipovic, do you recognise the signature that's on top of it that's for the SDS, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Okay. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Item 1, it says: "Distance themselves from any malevolent information regarding the presence of any armed groups or any formations in this area and from individuals writing malevolent and insulting anonymous letters and making malevolent and insulting telephone calls, and they condemn such behaviour." That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So what I asked you is whether you're aware that such an announcement was sent after these anonymous letters.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I know that we reacted because not a day passed without us being threatened. There were letters as well as telephone calls. But this is the first time that I see this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also told about an incident which took place in Pudin Han sometime in early April 1992. It was about a torching. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown DT28, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Filipovic, I'm being asked to ask you in turn to get nearer to the microphone when -- when you speak, because some of your -- yes, sometimes they can't hear exactly what you're saying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. In the transcript it says "BT". It's DT, "D".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. And I suppose Ms. Korner has exactly the same question as before too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no. I want to know where this document comes from, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this document is obviously a Prosecutor's document because it has the numbers, the ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I mean -- but it's one of our documents, and I understand it's put forward as an authentic document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the document. But I don't know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The assumption is that this is kind of an announcement on the radio, but we don't have any other information. It's a document that was handed over by the Prosecution. You can see here that people are being told that a certain Suvad Huskic was arrested, aka Mujin, and that he was the one who was responsible for the incident in Pudin Han. Do you remember that? First of all, do you know this Suvad Huskic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after this incident in April 1992 he was arrested -- because of this incident as a perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was arrested. I know that he's still in prison, Suvad Huskic. But if Your Honours will allow me, I will have to answer this because that night in Kljuc and in Pudin Han there were certain things that happened for which there is no terrorist organisation that could carry it out, that everything could happen at the same time. On that night windows on a house were also broken and Mujin was accused -- found responsible for everything. There were department shop windows that were broken. Everything happened within 4 kilometres, and it's impossible for one person to have done it all. But he was the usual suspect. He was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you do know that this Suvad Huskic was designated as a possible perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was accused. He was charged with that. I still don't think that he did it, but he was charged with that. I think that he also served a sentence for that. I don't know what his sentence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Filipovic, because here before the Chamber you said that while you were testifying, that this torching, this burning incident in Pudin Han, that this was done by the Serbs, that this is the Serbs who had set fire to hay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the situation in Kljuc was such that an incident situation was looked for actively, and this torching in Pudin Han was attempted to become that. So this was done, and only thanks to my -- the honesty of my late brother that the people didn't rebel, they didn't -- there was much damage done, and he managed, my late brother Omer, tried to calm them down, managed to calm them down. He said that it would be through the legal organs of power that something would be done, although the people were very upset.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this is before this Chamber you said that your assertion that this was done by the Serbs in order to provoke the incidents -- just what you said.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I still before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, according to this document, it is obvious that this is a Muslim who had done this, that there was a legal procedure taken, court proceedings, and he was charged with and he was convicted.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was convicted. I believe that that was done by Vlado Dimitrovic. And Mujin, he's been a criminal in Kljuc for 30 years. Whatever happens, I can do something. You can do something. He's always the usual suspect in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that what you're trying to say is that at the time you did not believe that the real perpetrator had been found but that this was a frame, that Suvad Huskic was framed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown DT29. And again, this has been -- this is the Prosecutor's document. The answer to Ms. Korner's question is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm very conscious of time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So are we.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the title says, that's an official communique about the event in Pudin Han which was signed by seven representatives of largest parties in Kljuc, is that correct, including your late brother Omer for the MBO? And just above his name, president of the SDA, I presume Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so. I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So let me ask you: You probably know your brother's signature.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this your brother's signature next to "MBO"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's difficult to say. You should find a different one so that we can compare it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was just asking whether this was his signature. So you cannot say for certain that this is your brother's signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the political parties -- that is, this is the first sentence -- that the parliamentary parties are fully support -- express full confidence in the organs of the Kljuc Public Security Station and the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, engaged in uncovering the perpetrators of the vandalistic fire in Pudin Han. The representatives of the parties consider this a crime and so the political parties consider this case settled." And this communique came presumably after Suvad Huskic was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that such an announcement, such a communique was broadcast, or issued?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to focus on early May 1992. You know about the events in Sarajevo of the 4th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here before this Chamber on several occasions during your testimony you talk about the transmitter, the repeater, and about the channels that you watched, TV channels. But if we can, I'd like us to clear that up a bit, elucidate. In any case, you were able to watch Sarajevo television first channel.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at home, until I was imprisoned, I could watch it. But there was -- there were some interference and there was often Austrian channel that was interfering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you watched Sarajevo first channel, the first programme of Sarajevo Television you watched?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was at home, when there was no interference with the Austrian programme, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the Kljuc municipality was also able to get Croatian stations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could only have the first programme, even now, of the federal television. And we are in a valley. Whoever has a satellite can watch the Croatian television. But you could do it if you are turned towards Krasulje. But the town of Kljuc doesn't have very many frequencies that it can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any case, when that man - I think his name was Pejic - when he destroyed the repeater of the second -- for the second channel of TV Belgrade, you were happy because you said that you were irritated by that channel, that it was an extremely biased channel.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't Pejic. It was Pajic. It's a Muslim last name, not a Serbian last name. Pejic would have been a Serbian last name. And even at that time, because I was so upset, I refused to pay a subscription for the Sarajevo Television. I even paid only half of the subscription, and I would even write on the pay form that I was only paying for the half of the subscription for the Sarajevo television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wasn't aware that the translation was still going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But whatever you said has not been noted into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I said is I think it's the appropriate time to take a break now because I am moving on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll break for 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, you're certainly aware of the fact that the Patriotic League was formed in 1991; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic was its commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know that in February negotiations -- consultations were arranged between the Patriotic League when plans were made for armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that now after the war. But at the time we were cut off from everything in Kljuc and we acted on an independent basis. We didn't receive orders from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I have understood you correctly, no one as far as you know , none of the Muslim leaders, no one from the leadership in Kljuc attended the meeting of the Patriotic League in February?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You formed the Patriotic League in Kljuc towards the end of 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time you formed headquarters for the Patriotic League in the municipality of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Crisis Staff. It was quite simply a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that Patriotic League staff you and your late brother, Omer, were part of this staff, Amir Abdic and Djeric Nerzet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Egrlic was also in it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us a little earlier on that you were cut off, that you didn't receive orders from anyone, and you worked on an independent basis so to speak; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the Patriotic League and the Patriotic League staff was also founded on your own?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not on our own. We knew what was happening. It wasn't done independently. But we hadn't received any instructions from anyone else. We simply wanted to be in that group of people who were prepared to mount resistance, but no one in particular came. You mentioned Sefer Halilovic. Sefer Halilovic didn't come to Kljuc and say that we had to do such and such a thing. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you hadn't received any instructions, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why do you say that you were cut off? We're talking about the year 1991. You founded the Patriotic League towards the end of 1991. That's what you said just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you that I was cut off in 1991 and in 1992 from Kljuc to Sarajevo. Where the Serbs -- that is to say, the SDS dominated, that was every several -- a vehicle could be checked every few kilometres, so that no one would set off for Sarajevo without good reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the witness be shown the map P446.1. And if it can be put on the ELMO, because I would need it for some time. A bit more, Mr. Usher, just a little bit, because I need -- I need the municipality to the far left. To the far left, yes. That's right. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, the fact that you avoided going to Sarajevo doesn't mean that you didn't have contact with Bihac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible to go to Bihac. But on the way to Bihac there were always check-ups in Laniste and Petrovac --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified earlier on, I said that I personally went to Prijedor to see Mr. Mirzad Mujadzic to tell him, since at the time he was a member of the state parliament, I went to tell him that something would happen and that the authorities in Sarajevo were trying to do something to protect us, because we had been left to ourselves. That's the only contact that I personally established with someone outside of Kljuc municipality. That's the only contact I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, the map can stay on the ELMO. It's -- I don't want the witness to point out anything on the ELMO. Just that we have it as a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Filipovic, you said that when you formed the Patriotic League towards the end of 1991, you said that from the beginning -- at the beginning you had about 50 members; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These were people who were ready, and we know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps that's inconvenient for you. Maybe you should turn the microphone towards yourself.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then in the course of your testimony you told us that in your opinion the situation deteriorated. And as this happened, your membership increased, the membership of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Only the core part and the first people who joined, we only considered these people to be the Patriotic League. And later on - and I'm not sure of the date- when the republican staff named Omer as the commander of the staff, then we formed the Territorial Defence. And after that membership increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you have addressed this topic. If I remember well, Omer on the 29th of April was appointed as the commander of the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but he was appointed by the Ministry. But it was known that Omer would be the commander one month before the official document was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was in the ministry in Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Efendic was the minister; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Efendic and Joko Doko. Those were the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how is it that in April 1992 you hadn't been cut off from Sarajevo and an order on this appointment could arise whereas in 1991 you were cut off?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, it was in your interest for a large number of people to join the Patriotic League; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have been happiest if everyone had joined, but that's not what the situation was from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you -- in order to achieve this, you popularised it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on what you mean by "popularise." We just told the people what would happen. And after a number of events, people realised what was happening, and they would join.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I remember correctly, you also spoke about how you made your announcements public, made your information public about what the Serbs were preparing and about how they were arming, et cetera; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We simply presented the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that given that the public had no access to this information, this is why you presented the information; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you obtained that information from certain Serbs after they had had a little too much to drink; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic, the situation was such that-- we Bosnians are a mixed people and regardless of what had happened, there were people who were ready to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But under the influence of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some under the influence of alcohol. Some because of many years of friendship they would say, "I can't tell you anything. You don't know me. You haven't seen me, but you heard this from Mr. X, et cetera," because there are always honest people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that in some way membership -- with regard to the membership of the Patriotic League, it was in your interest for the security situation in the municipality to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But just a minute ago you told us that as events unfolded and as the situation deteriorated, your membership grew. Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. But that's not what I wanted. I would still be happy even today if that had never happened, because first of all, I would be healthy. I wouldn't have had to go to hospital. And there would be 200.000 Bosnians still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't talking about your wish. I was talking about your interests.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a song about that, you know. Those weren't my wishes, not even for the third of us. I don't want to say that there any extremists who wished for such a situation. But in Kljuc, that was not case; that's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you to assume a post in the municipality of Bosnian Kljuc when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that right up until the time when we were informed from Sarajevo that the commander of the Territorial Defence had to be a graduate, up until that time I was a member of that Crisis Staff. And there was only one other person who had a higher rank than I did. And since I have finished the geodesics school -- I am a technician -- no one apart from my late brother wanted to assume this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly this morning when my colleague showed you Ismet Alagic's statement, you confirmed that you were present at that meeting which took place towards the end of April or at the beginning of May in Pudin Han.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at meetings. I don't hide this fact. I did participate in meetings. I went to meetings right up -- for as long as this was possible. But I think Mr. Muratagic's statement is from Manjaca. That's my opinion. Or from some detention centre until he went to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the meeting that followed immediately on the arrival of the order from Sarajevo in which your late brother was appointed as the Territorial Defence commander, the one in Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. This is how the situation was: When this note came saying that he had been appointed as commander, Jovo Banjac had already found out. He found out about it before Omer did. And it's absurd. Jovo Banjac, he's a Muslim who worked at the university -- a Muslim took it to him, not a Serb. That's what is absurd. So -- Jovo Banjac and the SDS leadership first found out that the Ministry had appointed Omer as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the decision was announced in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the communications centre. That's what it was called before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a -- I think the interpretation -- the translation was not really what I said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to add that it was received by fax, the order was received by fax, sent to the fax municipality, the municipality's fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. This clarifies the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll remind you of that meeting. The meeting was held from the 29th of April up until the 1st or 2nd of May in Pudin Han, between these dates, in the headquarters -- in the centre where you and your late brother were, the brothers Egrlic, Asim and Ibrahim, Amir Abdic, Djeric Nerzet, Salih Salihovic, Muratagic Ismet and the military commander from the territory of the municipality. You remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had several such meetings. Whenever it was possible to meet, we would meet. And in military terms, so to speak, there were reports on what was happening on the situation. So I don't know about that specific case, but there were several such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to refresh your memory. At that meeting your late brother, Omer, in his introductory remark informed all of you of the conclusions of the meeting in Sanski Most and informed you of the instructions he had received from the commander of the Cazinska region Territorial Defence. Does this help you remember?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that one of the meetings they said that policemen who refused to pledge their loyalty to the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina, then their families would receive their salaries from the Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina regardless of the fact that they weren't working. I remember that they mentioned this at one meeting. And I don't know anything else. I know that all our plans were that if war should break out, we'd be able to receive help from Bihac, first of all, before receiving help from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know of or did you know Hajrudin Osmanagic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the regional staff of the TO of the Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that name. As for the leadership in Bihac that I knew, who were my friends, who were friends of my family, this was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Safet Hidic from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, can you repeat these two name, please, these last two name that is you mentioned, because one of them the interpreters did not catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Late Dr. Irfan Ljubijankic. He was killed in the war. He was Minister of foreign affairs of BH, and the other one is also late Safet Hidic. One is from Bihac and the other one is from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't remember specifically about the meeting and the instructions that your late brother received from the commander of the TO Cazin region.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps the meeting at which your plans were made and when your late brother said that the villages of Velecevo and Dubocani should -- including the town itself could not be counted on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. When we were making the plan of the defence, this was the situation that required this. This part could not be counted on, because there was a lot of mixed population. And just when you asked me something earlier, what I remember is that once my brother and Asim went to Kladovo to Fikret Abdic, to see him. But I don't know what they negotiated with him, but I do know that they went once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, these two villages, Velecevo and Dubocani, these villages had predominantly Muslim population, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. But they were surround by Serbian villages. And towards Ribnik -- this was only after the Dayton Agreement that they were returned to the Federation. But at the end of the war they were part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you as the Patriotic League or the Territorial Defence did not have much of a support there, did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were people, Mr. Zecevic, who wanted to defend their state, their neighbourhood, but territorially speaking we couldn't count on them because had we appeared in the Dubocani of Velecevo to a meeting, if you lived there and if we came to see you for coffee, on this very same day we would have been arrested and people would say, "Here they are. They are preparing something." So it was from this particular point of view that we thought that we couldn't count on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I presume that for reasons of secrecy of your preparations the contacts that you had with military commanders from various regions, these contacts were kept only through Nerzet Djeric. Is that correct? Do you remember that decision of yours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nirzet Djeric, aka Kajdzo, was also a reserve officer and all the inhabited places would contact with Kajdzo. They would speak with him. But this was all privately. Somebody would meet up and then this message would be passed on to him. It was such a situation that we really couldn't afford to have more people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that what was also established was a location where couriers or messengers met, which was the unfinished house of Omer --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your decision that the financing -- that the public security station of Bosanski Kljuc would be financed through the Bihac bank in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said. That's what I said, that the policemen were promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you just said? Oh, you mean the Bosnian policemen were promised that they would be financed by the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the meeting where you as the Crisis Staff or the Patriotic League, you issued instructions for establishment of armed formations in villages with Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't establish formations. Because it was a crisis, each village had their own sentries, had their own guards. So it was in their own initiative that people had sentries organised. And then once they did it, they would come to us and say, "Is this okay what we are doing?" So this is what we tried, was that -- that Serbs would also join these sentries. For instance, there is -- in Velagici there is a village of Kopjenica where there is Serbs, and we said that they shouldn't think that they would be attacked so it would be good to be in contact with them, because they also had their own sentries, so there wouldn't be some stupidity that happened, some shooting.
